title: SCO Summit Leaves Proposed Development Bank Unresolved as India Balances Bloc Ties
excerpt: The Bishkek summit delivered institutional reforms and a 28-document package, but the proposed SCO Development Bank remains without a founding agreement, capital structure, or headquarters.
body:
• The SCO summit in Bishkek adopted 28 documents including the Bishkek Declaration marking the bloc's 25th anniversary, but stopped short of launching the proposed Development Bank.
  • Both Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan made competing bids to host the bank's headquarters, underscoring how much remains unsettled on governance, capital, and membership.
  • India's Prime Minister Modi used his bilateral meeting with Putin to call for moving "from endless war to an end to the war" on Ukraine — the sharpest public statement on the conflict at the summit.
  • Turkey's President Erdogan signaled Ankara may consider full SCO membership while maintaining NATO ties, a development that could reshape the bloc's strategic balance.

Leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization wrapped up a two-day summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on September 1, adopting a sweeping 28-document package of institutional reforms while leaving the bloc's most consequential economic proposal — a new Development Bank — without a founding agreement, capital commitment, or launch date.

The summit brought together Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and leaders from the SCO's other member states as the organization marked its 25th anniversary.

A Bank Without a Home

The Bishkek Declaration recorded progress toward creating the Development Bank "among interested member states," but the language was qualified. Members reached political consensus on the concept at last year's Tianjin summit, yet the bank's membership structure, governance model, capitalization, and location remain under negotiation, according to the Times of Central Asia.

https://x.com/Pacific_Dialog/status/2095546751315058789

Two competing headquarters bids emerged at Bishkek. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who used his country's chairmanship to push the initiative, urged members to reach a practical decision and invited them to use Kyrgyzstan's Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory for joint projects. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev countered with his own offer.

"If there is consensus among the member states, Kazakhstan could host this institution, its headquarters."

— Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, President of Kazakhstan

India's position on the bank has been measured. New Delhi views the SCO as one of several overlapping platforms through which it can maximize its own strategic agency, rather than a bloc demanding exclusive alignment, analysts say. The financial proposals have greater strategic relevance for Moscow and Tehran, which face restrictions on established financial channels, according to SpecialEurasia.

Modi on Ukraine, Terrorism

Ukraine went unmentioned in the formal Bishkek Declaration, but the sharpest public remarks on the war came during Modi's bilateral meeting with Putin.

"Every day spent on war pushes humanity backwards, whereas every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

Putin replied that Russia was moving along that path, according to a Kremlin transcript. In his summit address, Modi also demanded an end to double standards on terrorism and said connectivity projects must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity — language widely interpreted as a reference to China's Belt and Road Initiative, which passes through Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

Institutional Overhaul

The summit approved amendments to the SCO's 2002 Charter and regulations for two new security bodies: a Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats, and the executive committee of an Anti-Drug Center in Dushanbe. Programs against synthetic narcotics through 2030 and a 2026–2030 roadmap for ports and logistics centers were also adopted.

The declaration retained strong language on Iran, condemning military strikes on Iranian territory and backing Tehran's sovereignty. On Afghanistan, members supported an independent, neutral, and peaceful state free of terrorism. A separate statement on disaster relief — a Kyrgyz priority — was adopted, though funding details remain unclear.

Turkey's Signal

In a development that could reshape the bloc's strategic makeup, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on September 2 that Turkey would consider full SCO membership while maintaining its NATO and Western relationships. The statement signals that some nations view closer SCO engagement as compatible with existing Western alliances rather than a strategic realignment.

What's Next

Pakistan assumes the SCO chairmanship for 2026–2027 and is expected to host the next heads-of-state summit in Islamabad. The Bishkek meeting leaves the organization with an enlarged institutional framework and a long list of sectoral programs, but the Development Bank — potentially the SCO's most significant economic institution — remains a proposal rather than an operating lender.
